title: Spring Core Quick Revision: Beans, Injection, Config and Profiles
summary: Quick revision notes on the Spring container and bean model, stereotype annotations, constructor injection, scopes and lifecycle, Java configuration, Boot auto-configuration and starters, and profiles with externalized properties.

chapters.title: Spring Container and Bean Mental Model
points: A bean is an object created, wired and managed by the IoC container; inversion of control means the container builds objects and supplies their dependencies instead of your code calling new
BeanFactory is the basic container with lazy bean creation; ApplicationContext adds events, i18n, property resolution and eager singleton creation at startup, and is what you use in practice
Container startup flow: read configuration (annotations or Java config), build BeanDefinitions, instantiate beans, inject dependencies, run initialization callbacks
Component scanning: @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan, which finds stereotype classes in its own package and sub-packages only; classes outside that tree are silently skipped
Retrieve a bean by type via context.getBean(Type.class), but prefer injection; calling getBean in business code is the service locator anti-pattern

chapters.title: Stereotypes and Constructor Injection
points: @Component is the generic stereotype; @Service (business logic) and @Repository (persistence) are specializations with the same registration behavior, and @Controller/@RestController serve the web layer
@Repository also enables translation of persistence exceptions (such as SQLException) into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy
Constructor injection: declare dependencies as final constructor parameters; with a single constructor, @Autowired is optional since Spring 4.3

Constructor injection beats field injection because dependencies are immutable, required, testable with plain new, and the object is never half-built; field injection hides dependencies and needs reflection or a container to test
Two beans of the same type cause NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException; resolve with @Primary on the default bean or @Qualifier("name") at the injection point
Circular constructor dependencies (A needs B, B needs A) fail at startup with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; fix by redesigning, not by switching to field injection

chapters.title: Bean Scopes and Lifecycle
points: Default scope is singleton: one shared instance per container, not per JVM, so singleton beans must be stateless or thread-safe
prototype creates a new instance on every injection or lookup, and Spring does not call destroy callbacks for prototype beans; request, session and application scopes are web-only
Injecting a prototype or request-scoped bean into a singleton gives you a single instance frozen at injection time; fix with ObjectProvider<T>, or @Scope(proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS)

Lifecycle order: instantiate, inject dependencies, @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, ready for use, @PreDestroy, destroy; use @PostConstruct for init that needs injected fields, never the constructor
Lazy initialization with @Lazy defers creation until first use, which moves wiring errors from startup to runtime

chapters.title: @Configuration and @Bean
points: @Configuration marks a class holding @Bean methods; each method's return value is registered as a bean named after the method, and the class is CGLIB-proxied so repeated bean-method calls return the same singleton
Use @Bean for third-party classes you cannot annotate (ObjectMapper, RestTemplate, DataSource); use stereotype annotations for your own classes
@Bean method parameters are injected automatically, so wire dependencies by declaring them as arguments rather than calling other bean methods
@Bean(initMethod, destroyMethod) hooks lifecycle callbacks for third-party objects, and @Bean methods can be conditional with @ConditionalOnMissingBean or @Profile
@Component with @Bean methods is lite mode: no proxying, so inter-bean method calls create new instances; use @Configuration when beans call each other

chapters.title: Auto-Configuration, Starters, Profiles and Properties
points: A starter (spring-boot-starter-web, -data-jpa, -test) is a dependency bundle that pulls in a compatible set of libraries with managed versions; it contains no logic itself

Auto-configuration is registered in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports and applies conditionally with @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean and @ConditionalOnProperty
Your own bean of the same type overrides the auto-configured default because of @ConditionalOnMissingBean; debug what applied with --debug or the conditions report

Properties live in application.properties or application.yml; precedence from highest: command-line args, environment variables, profile-specific files, then default application file; inject with @Value("${key:default}") or type-safe @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")

Profiles: set spring.profiles.active=prod (or SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE env var), load application-prod.yml on top of the defaults, and gate beans with @Profile("dev"); never commit secrets in property files

chapters.title: Spring Core Cheat Sheet
points: Annotation map: @Component/@Service/@Repository/@Controller register beans; @Configuration plus @Bean for third-party objects; @Primary and @Qualifier choose among candidates
Injection rules: constructor for required dependencies, final fields, one constructor needs no @Autowired; setter only for optional ones
Scope table: singleton (default, shared), prototype (new per request, no destroy), request, session, application (web only)
Lifecycle one-liner: construct, inject, @PostConstruct, in use, @PreDestroy; Boot flow: starter on classpath, auto-config condition matches, your bean overrides it
Config one-liner: properties precedence is CLI, env, profile file, default file; activate with spring.profiles.active; type-safe binding via @ConfigurationProperties
